question: Match the device: 50, 51, and 87.
choices: 50 time overcurrent, 51 instantaneous, 87 lockout
50 instantaneous overcurrent, 51 time overcurrent, 87 differential
50 differential, 51 distance, 87 frequency
50 undervoltage, 51 overvoltage, 87 reclosing
explanation: ATS 7.9.1 names 50 as instantaneous overcurrent, 51 as time overcurrent, and 87 as differential. 86 is the lockout and is not one of those three. IEEE C37.113-2015 clause 3.2 says its device numbers follow IEEE C37.2; the names used here are the ones printed in the ATS list.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1 devices 50, 51, and 87; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 3.2 (numbers follow IEEE C37.2)

question: ATS 7.9.1 tells you to determine which of the following on an 87 differential?
choices: Only the target color
Operating-unit pickup, restraint, slope, and harmonic restraint
The transformer's oil interfacial tension
A 10-minute polarization index of the relay case only
explanation: ATS 7.9.1 tells you to determine harmonic restraint on an 87, along with pickup, slope, and the restraint characteristic. It does not name the second harmonic in that sentence. IEEE C37.91-2021 clause 7.3.4.2 is where harmonic restraint is used so magnetizing inrush does not trip the differential, and clause 6.5.3 says that inrush is rich in harmonics, particularly the second.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 87; ref. IEEE C37.91-2021, clauses 6.5.3 and 7.3.4.2

question: Functional checks in ATS 7.9.1 include proving that relay contacts perform which scheme jobs?
choices: Breaker trip, close inhibit, 86 lockout, and alarms
Only the front-panel lamp test
Oil sampling and a turns-ratio test
A Wenner soil box on the station ground
explanation: The functional paragraph names breaker trip tests, close inhibit, 86 lockout tests, and alarm functions, and points at Section 8. A relay that asserts in the test set but never moves the trip wire is not finished.

question: A CT primary is carrying load and someone opens the secondary at the terminal block. The hazard is:
choices: The secondary voltage collapses to zero and is safe to hold
The secondary can develop a dangerous voltage while it tries to maintain ampere-turns
Only the revenue meter is affected; the leads stay at a few volts
The CT automatically shorts itself inside the head
explanation: An open CT secondary with primary current flowing can rise to a hazardous voltage. Short the secondary or leave it on its burden before the primary is energized. ATS also requires exactly one secondary ground, at the place the drawings show.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (open CT secondary); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.9

question: You need to see whether an 86 contact is in the breaker close circuit. Which drawing actually shows the coil and the contact?
choices: The one-line, because it shows every contact
The control schematic (or elementary), not the one-line
The site plot plan
The oil lab report
explanation: A one-line shows the power path and the device numbers. The control schematic shows coils, a and b contacts, and how a lockout is inserted into trip and close. Asking a one-line to carry the close-permissive contact is the print trap.

question: ATS 7.22.1 for an engine generator tells you to verify, as the application requires:
choices: Only the fuel-filter color
Phase rotation, phasing, and synchronized operation
That synchronization is optional if the breaker is closed fast
Winding resistance instead of rotation
explanation: 7.22.1.B.3 and the matching test-value line require phase rotation, phasing, and synchronizing to match the system design. Closing a generator onto a live bus with the wrong rotation is a fault, not a commissioning footnote.

question: A 51 contact energizes an 86 lockout, and an 86 contact energizes the breaker trip coil. In that path, what operates first?
choices: The 86 coil
The 52 trip coil
The 51 element
The breaker springs, before any relay
explanation: The 51 has to pick up and close its contact before the 86 coil is energized. The 86 then latches mechanically, and its contact energizes the trip coil, so the breaker opens third in this path. An 86 is hand-reset. It does not merely seal in electrically, and resetting the breaker does not reset the lockout.

question: An 86 b contact is in the close-permissive string. The lockout trips (coil picked up). That b contact:
choices: Closes and allows a close
Opens and blocks closing until the lockout is reset
Does not change, because b contacts are not used in trip circuits
Becomes an a contact automatically
explanation: A b contact is closed when the device is de-energized and open when the device is picked up. A tripped 86 opens its b contact and removes close permission. An a contact would do the opposite and is the one you would use to energize a trip or an alarm when the lockout operates.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (a and b contacts); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1.B.4

question: ATS 7.9.1’s time-overcurrent (51) test is:
choices: Pickup only
Minimum pickup, and time at two points on the curve
A single instantaneous shot
Slope and harmonic restraint
explanation: The 51 list is minimum pickup and time delay at two points on the curve. Slope and harmonic restraint are the 87 list. One point cannot show that the curve is the one in the study.

question: A directional overcurrent (67) test in ATS 7.9.1 includes:
choices: Only the target reset
Directional-unit pickup at maximum torque angle, the closing zone, and the overcurrent unit
Oil dielectric of the case
A 10-minute polarization index
explanation: Direction is the point of a 67. Pickup at the maximum-torque angle, the zone where the contact closes, and the overcurrent unit all belong in that test. A non-directional 51 will not catch a reversed polarizing circuit.

question: On a microprocessor feeder relay, ATS 7.9.2 says element timing is judged against:
choices: One NETA percent for every relay
The manufacturer’s recommended tolerances
Table 100.7
The inspector’s stopwatch habit
explanation: 7.9.2.D.4 says protection elements should operate within the manufacturer’s recommended tolerances. A 50 element and a 51 element on the same relay can have different published bands. Do not borrow Table 100.7 from molded-case breakers.

question: Restoring a relay test switch after injection, the safe order is:
choices: Close the trip poles first so the breaker is protected while CTs are still open
Close the trip poles last, after the current circuits are restored
Leave the CT shorting blade open as a spare
Open the trip poles and go home
explanation: On the way in, open the trip circuit first so a stray assertion does not trip the breaker, and let the CT shorting blade make before the relay current circuit opens. On the way out, restore the current circuits and close the trip poles last. That order is the test-switch maker's practice: the trip poles open first, and the CT short is make-before-break. ATS-2025 7.10.1.A.7 is the check that the grounding and shorting connections actually make contact. Leaving a CT secondary open under load is the hazard.
reference: ABB FT-1/FT-14 Flexitest product guide 1VAC394641-PG Rev K; engineering fundamentals; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.A.7

question: Settings and logic in a microprocessor relay should agree with:
choices: Whatever was found, because changing it is outside testing
The most recent engineered setting file
Factory default
The previous technician’s memory
explanation: ATS 7.9.2 says settings and logic should agree with the latest engineered setting files. As-found that does not match gets written down. As-left is the file, not a dial you liked during the test.

question: A SEL-751-class feeder relay publishes its own pickup and timing tolerances. Those numbers are:
choices: Replaced by a single NETA percent
What you test against for that relay, because 7.9.2 points at the manufacturer
Taken from Table 100.8
Optional if metering looks right
explanation: The percent on the relay manual is that relay’s band. ATS 7.9.2.D.4 tells you to use the manufacturer’s recommended tolerances. Quoting another relay’s ±3% or a breaker’s Table 100.8 is the wrong document.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2.D.4; element tolerances per the relay manufacturer

question: Two lockout relays, 86-1 and 86-2, both trip the same breaker and each has a b contact in the close circuit. After a trip, close permissive returns when:
choices: Either lockout is reset
Both lockouts are reset
The breaker is closed once, which resets both
The 51 target is cleared
explanation: Each b contact is open while its coil is picked up. Series permissives mean both must be reset. Resetting one and closing into the other lockout is how a second trip surprises people.

question: Device 25, synchronism check, in a generator breaker close scheme should:
choices: Close the breaker by itself as soon as frequency is near
Block the close until voltage, angle, and slip are inside the setting
Replace the 86
Be defeated for the first parallel
explanation: 25 supervises the close. It does not replace the operator or the 86. ATS 7.22.1 still wants phase rotation, phasing, and synchronizing proved. Bypassing 25 for “the first time” is how out-of-phase closes happen.

question: A close scheme uses an 86 b contact and a 52 b contact in series. The breaker is closed and the lockout is reset. The 52 b contact is:
choices: Closed, because the breaker is closed
Open, because a b contact opens when the breaker is closed
A trip contact
Irrelevant until the 51 times out
explanation: A b contact is closed only while its device is dropped out. A closed breaker has opened its 52b contact. In series with the close coil, that contact allows a close only while the breaker is open, and it cuts the close coil off once the breaker closes. Anti-pump is a separate function, usually a 52Y relay, that blocks a second close while the close signal is still held. The 86 b contact is closed only while the lockout is reset.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (a and b contact logic)

question: Before you time a microprocessor relay element, ATS 7.9.2 expects you to:
choices: Skip settings and only ramp current
Confirm settings and logic match the latest engineered file
Set every pickup to the minimum
Megger the relay at 10 kV
explanation: Settings and logic should agree with the most recent engineered setting files. A perfect timing shot on the wrong file is not a passing relay. Element tolerances then come from the manufacturer, not from a generic percent.

question: A relay test set’s current output belongs:
choices: On the live CT secondary while the primary is in service
On the relay side of an open, shorted test switch, with the CT shorted
Across the breaker primary poles
On the station ground only
explanation: You inject into the relay, not into a CT that is still connected to a live primary. The test switch shorts the CT before the relay circuit opens. ATS 7.9.2 then judges the element against the manufacturer’s tolerance.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2.D.4; ABB FT Flexitest product guide

question: SEL-751-class feeder relays publish pickup and timing bands in the data sheet. ATS 7.9.2 tells you to:
choices: Ignore those bands and use ±10% for every element
Test to the manufacturer’s tolerances for the element you enabled
Use Table 100.8
Skip timing if the metering screen matches
explanation: A 50 element and a 51 element do not share one percent. The data sheet is that relay’s band. 7.9.2.D.4 points at the manufacturer’s recommended tolerances, and the settings still have to match the study.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2.D.4; SEL-751 data sheet, per manufacturer instructions

question: A close circuit is supervised by device 25 and by an 86 b contact. The breaker should close only when:
choices: Either one is satisfied
Sync-check allows it and the lockout is reset
The 51 is picked up
The test set is still connected
explanation: 25 permits the close when the two systems match. The 86 b contact is closed only while the lockout is reset. Both have to be true. Resetting the breaker handle does not reset the 86.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 21 is:
choices: A distance relay
A lockout relay
A frequency relay
A reclosing relay
explanation: 21 is distance. 81 is frequency, 79 is reclosing, and 86 is the lockout used on schematics. IEEE C37.113-2015 clause 3.2 uses this same numbering system.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 21; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 3.2

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 67 is:
choices: Directional overcurrent
Undervoltage
Differential
Sync check
explanation: 67 is directional overcurrent. 27 is undervoltage, 87 is differential, and 25 is sync check. The test list for 67 includes the directional unit, not an oil sample.

question: Setting up a test plan for a non-piloted zone 1 distance element, you expect its reach to be set so that it:
choices: Reaches past the next line
Does not overreach the remote terminal
Trips only after zone 3
Ignores the remote bus on purpose by using no voltage
explanation: Zone 1 is instantaneous. If it sees past the remote bus it trips for a fault that belongs to the next zone. ATS 7.9.1 tests the reach of a 21; this clause is the reason that reach stops short of the far terminal.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 21; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 5.5.2

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 40 is:
choices: Loss of field, tested as an impedance relay
A reclosing relay
A frequency relay
A sudden-pressure relay
explanation: 40 is loss of field. The tests include torque angle, reach, offset, and the impedance circle. 63 is sudden pressure, 79 is reclosing, and 81 is frequency.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 79 is:
choices: Reclosing
Distance
Differential
Undervoltage
explanation: 79 is the reclosing relay. 21 is distance, 87 is differential, and 27 is undervoltage. A reclose attempt is not a zone 1 reach.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 81 is:
choices: Frequency
Sync check
Pilot-wire monitor
Ground detector
explanation: 81 is frequency. 25 is sync check, 85 is the pilot-wire monitor, and 64 is the ground detector. The 81 tests include pickup and time delay, not a gas sample.

question: On a step-distance line relay you're testing, zone 2 is:
choices: The instantaneous element that must reach the next bus
Time-delayed protection from the end of zone 1 to the end of the line, and backup if zone 1 fails
A differential zone bounded only by the transformer CTs
The reclosing timer
explanation: Zone 1 covers part of the line without delay and must not overreach. Zone 2 picks up the rest of the line on a delay and also covers a failed zone 1. Zone 3 reaches beyond zone 1 as further backup. ATS tests the 21 reach; this clause is why the zones are not the same setting.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 21; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 4.6

question: When you test distance-relay reach, the reach is measured from:
choices: The current-transformer location only
The voltage-transformer location, with direction set by the current transformers
The remote bus, always
The station battery
explanation: The ohms start at the VT. The CT decides which way is forward. Line-side VTs and CTs see the line directly. Low-side instruments add the transformer impedance and the wye-delta shift, which the setting has to include. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 21; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 5.5.2.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 21; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 5.5.2

question: An ATS 6.6 harmonic-study report is supposed to include:
choices: Only a single power-factor number
Voltage and current distortion compared with IEEE 519, with exceedances flagged, and an impedance-versus-frequency plot
A dissolved-gas chromatogram
The crew leader’s ETT card
explanation: Item 5 of the report is the distortion table against IEEE 519. Item 6 is the resonance plot. Item 7 checks transformer capability under the nonsinusoidal current using IEEE C57.110. A passing power factor does not answer any of those.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 6.6, study report items 5 and 6; ref. IEEE 519-2022

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 27 is:
choices: Undervoltage
Overvoltage
Distance
Differential
explanation: 27 is undervoltage. 59 is overvoltage. They are not a matched pair you can swap on a print. 21 and 87 are impedance and differential.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 59 is:
choices: Overvoltage
Undervoltage
Sync check
Reclosing
explanation: 59 is overvoltage. 27 is undervoltage, 25 is sync check, and 79 is reclosing. An overvoltage element does not check synchronism.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 25 is:
choices: Sync check
Distance
Frequency
Sudden pressure
explanation: 25 supervises a close when two systems have to match. It is not the distance element and not the frequency element. 63 is sudden pressure.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 63 is:
choices: Transformer sudden pressure
A pilot-wire monitor
A thermal RTD relay
Breaker failure
explanation: 63 is sudden pressure. 85 is the pilot-wire monitor, 49T is the RTD temperature relay, and 50BF is breaker failure. A sudden-pressure trip is a mechanical fault detector, not a time-overcurrent curve.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 46 is:
choices: Current balance
Phase-sequence voltage
Loss of field
Ground detector
explanation: 46 is current balance. 47 is phase-sequence or phase-balance voltage, 40 is loss of field, and 64 is the ground detector. The 46 tests include pickup of each unit and slope.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 32 is:
choices: Directional power
Distance
Differential
Reclosing
explanation: 32 is directional power. It is the element that looks at watts in a direction, not a distance reach and not a reclose. 21, 87, and 79 are those other jobs.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 47 is:
choices: Phase-sequence or phase-balance voltage
Current balance
Loss of field
Instantaneous overcurrent
explanation: 47 looks at voltage sequence. 46 is current balance, 40 is loss of field, and 50 is instantaneous overcurrent. A reversed phase rotation is a 47 problem, not a 50 pickup.

question: On a protection one-line, the boundary of a relay's protection zone is set by:
choices: The voltage-transformer nameplate alone
Where the current transformers are, because those currents define the zone
The paint on the lineup
The reclosing timer
explanation: The CTs are the edges of the zone. Overlap is intentional so a fault on a boundary still falls in a zone. ATS 7.9.1 tests the 87 that lives inside those boundaries; this clause is why the CT location is not cosmetic.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 87; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 4.4

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 24 is:
choices: Volts per hertz
Distance
Reclosing
Frequency
explanation: 24 is volts per hertz, the overexcitation element. 21 is distance, 79 is reclosing, and 81 is frequency. Overexcitation is not a zone reach.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 49T is:
choices: An RTD temperature relay
A thermal replica of current
Breaker failure
Sync check
explanation: 49T is the temperature relay that looks at RTD resistance. 49R is the thermal replica driven by current. 50BF is breaker failure. The 49T tests are trip resistance and reset resistance.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 60 is:
choices: Voltage balance
Current balance
Ground detector
Pilot wire
explanation: 60 compares voltages. 46 compares currents. 64 is the ground detector and 85 is the pilot-wire monitor. A blown VT fuse is the sort of unbalance a 60 is there to see.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 64 is:
choices: A ground detector
A differential
A distance element
A frequency element
explanation: 64 is the ground detector. 87 is differential, 21 is distance, and 81 is frequency. A ground detector on an ungrounded system is not a transformer differential.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 85 is:
choices: A pilot-wire monitor
A reclosing relay
Sudden pressure
Volts per hertz
explanation: 85 supervises the pilot channel. 79 recloses, 63 is sudden pressure, and 24 is volts per hertz. A dead pilot channel is not a successful pilot scheme.

question: A line panel has main 1 and main 2 relays. What are they?
choices: Two names for the same relay
Redundant schemes so one failed component does not remove all protection for that circuit
Zone 1 and zone 3 of a single distance relay
The owner’s short-circuit study and the test report
explanation: Local redundancy means a second scheme at the same terminal. Remote backup is a relay at another station, which is slower and less selective. ATS still tests each scheme against its settings file.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 4.6

question: A line is protected by a DUTT scheme only. With the remote breaker open for maintenance, you simulate a fault near the remote end, past the local zone 1 reach. What should the test show?
choices: A high-speed trip from a received transfer-trip signal
No pilot trip; only time-delayed backup clears it
An instantaneous trip from a local overreaching element
A block signal that stops every trip, including backup
explanation: DUTT only trips fast from underreaching elements, either the local one or the far-end one keying a transfer trip. With the remote breaker open, nothing at the far end sees the fault, and the local zone 1 stops short of it. Only the time-delayed backup clears it. The same gap opens if the channel fails, which is why C37.113 treats DUTT mostly as a supplement to another pilot scheme. Test the channel and the backup timers in the same pass.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1.B.3, item 2 (device 21) and 7.9.2.B.5.4; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clauses 4.8.7 and 6.3.5.2

question: End-to-end testing a POTT line: with both breakers closed, a simulated internal fault trips both ends at high speed. With the remote breaker open, the local end trips only on its time-delayed zone. What is the most likely gap?
choices: The local overreaching element is set short of the remote bus
POTT cannot trip with one breaker open, so nothing can be done
No remote 52b keying or echo, so no permissive is sent
The local zone 1 timer is set too long
explanation: POTT trips only when the local overreaching element picks up and a permissive comes back from the far end. An open remote breaker carries no fault current, so its element never keys the channel unless 52b keying or open-breaker echo does it for it. C37.113 calls for one of those. The both-closed test already proved the reach and the channel. ATS 7.9.2.B.5.3 has you check that logic against the owner’s narrative.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2.B.5.3 and B.5.4; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clauses 6.3.5.4 and 6.3.5.8

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 50BF is:
choices: Breaker failure
Instantaneous overcurrent with no breaker-failure logic
Bus differential
Reclosing
explanation: 50BF is breaker failure in the ATS 7.9.1 list. A plain 50 is instantaneous overcurrent, and 79 is reclosing. Breaker failure has its own test items in that list.

question: In the ATS 7.9.1 list, device 46N is:
choices: Negative-sequence current
Phase-balance voltage
Ground detector
Volts per hertz
explanation: 46N is negative-sequence current, with an alarm, a trip, and an I2-squared-t curve. 47 is the voltage phase-sequence relay. 64 is the ground detector and 24 is volts per hertz.

question: ATS 7.22.1.B.2 tests protective relays on an engine generator:
choices: In accordance with section 7.9
By a polarization index of the relay case
Only if they are device 87
As part of NFPA 70E glove inspection
explanation: Generator relays are not a private test. They go through section 7.9, element by element, against the settings. The machine insulation test stays in the IEEE 43 item.

question: Before acceptance tests, ATS-2025 section 4.1 requires the owner to provide:
choices: A short-circuit study, a coordination study, and the protective-device settings
Only the oil sample
A waiver of the interlock checks
The test technician’s personal lock
explanation: Those three documents are how the installed fuses, breakers, and relays are judged. Without them, a perfect timing shot may be a shot at the wrong setting. Site hazard training is a separate item in the same section.

question: On a transmission line scheme, what is the difference between local backup and remote backup?
choices: Local backup is at the line’s own substations; remote backup is at other substations
Local backup is always zone 3 and remote backup is zone 1
They are two names for main 1
Remote backup is faster and more selective
explanation: Local backup, including a second scheme at the same terminal, avoids the delay and the loss of selectivity that come with clearing a fault from another station. Remote backup is that other station. Neither one deletes the need to test the settings. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 4.6.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2; ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clause 4.6

question: A line ends in a wye-delta transformer. The distance relay uses the line-side VTs but the transformer low-side CTs, and the setting sheet turns on zero-sequence-compensated ground distance for line ground faults. What do you flag in the settings review?
choices: Low-side CTs miss line zero-sequence, so ground elements are not reliable
Nothing; reach is measured from the CTs, so the low-side CTs are correct
Only the 30° shift; once that is corrected, ground distance works normally
Ground distance should overreach the remote bus to make up for it
explanation: With current taken from the delta side, the line’s zero-sequence current for a line-side ground fault isn’t measured. Compensated ground distance, zero-sequence directional, and ground overcurrent elements on those CTs aren’t dependable. The 30° wye-delta shift does need correcting, but that fixes angle, not the missing zero sequence. Reach is measured from the VTs, and zone 1 still must not reach the remote bus. This is why C37.113 prefers line-side CTs and VTs.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.2.A.8 and 7.9.1.B.3, item 2 (device 21); ref. IEEE C37.113-2015, clauses 5.5.2 and 5.5.4

question: Why does a transformer differential relay use harmonic restraint?
choices: The relay can be set more sensitively without tripping on inrush
Inrush is ignored by deleting the slope
The second harmonic forces a trip
Percentage restraint is removed
explanation: Restraint, or blocking, recognizes inrush and lets the operating pickup stay low for real faults. ATS 7.9.1 says to determine that harmonic restraint. It does not tell you to turn it off to make the relay trip faster on energizing.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 87; ref. IEEE C37.91-2021, clause 7.3.4.2.1

question: When does false differential current on a transformer differential get worse?
choices: The CT ratios match exactly and the tap changer never moves
CT ratios cannot be matched, and an on-load tap changer moves the ratio further
The relay has percentage restraint
Harmonic restraint is in service
explanation: A ratio that is only close still leaves operating current. A load tap changer makes the mismatch move. If someone changes a de-energized tap and does not update the relay, the mismatch grows again. ATS 7.9.1 has you determine the slope that is supposed to ride through that through-fault current.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 87; ref. IEEE C37.91-2021, clause 6.5.2

question: Two parallel transformers share one 87 zone. T1 is in service, and the 87 trips when T2 is energized. The event shows little second harmonic. T2 passes its tests and energizes fine with T1 off, and the 87’s harmonic restraint tests good. Most likely cause and fix?
choices: Sympathetic inrush; give each transformer its own 87
An internal fault in T2; keep it out of service
CT polarity on T2 is reversed; swap the leads
The slope is too low; raise it until energizing rides through
explanation: When a unit is switched in beside one already energized, inrush flows in both on opposite half-cycles. The net current into a zone around both can be close to fundamental, so harmonic restraint doesn’t block it, and the event can run long. C37.91 recommends a separate differential for each parallel unit, which also recovers the sensitivity lost by sizing the CTs for both. Reversed polarity would trip on load, and T2’s clean tests argue against a fault.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1.B.3, item 25 (device 87); ref. IEEE C37.91-2021, clauses 6.5.3 and 7.3.8

question: On an electromechanical differential for a delta-wye transformer, the wye-side CTs are connected in delta to:
choices: Increase the CT burden to three times on purpose, with no other reason
Keep zero-sequence current out of the differential when a ground fault is on the wye circuit
Measure the knee
Replace harmonic restraint
explanation: Zero-sequence current flows in the grounded wye and circulates in the transformer delta, so it does not come out the delta terminals. Delta CTs on the wye side trap that current so the relay does not see a false mismatch. Some relays remove the zero sequence in software instead. ATS 7.9.1 tests the 87 that depends on this balance.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 87; ref. IEEE C37.91-2021, clause 6.4.3

question: An NFPA 70B-2026 field-test record has to include:
choices: Only pass or fail
Who tested, the equipment identity and nameplate, the conditions, the date, and the test, plus criteria, as-found and as-left values, and comments where those apply
The manufacturer's entire manual
A polarization index on every record
explanation: The record names who tested, what was tested, the conditions, the date, and which test was run. Criteria, as-found and as-left values, and comments or recommendations are required where they apply, not as a filled box on every line. A bare pass or fail with none of that cannot support the next interval.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 adjusts a maintenance interval by:
choices: Leaving it fixed no matter what fails
Letting a failure analysis decide whether a shorter interval is needed, allowing a risk-based change, and documenting a longer interval after more than two problem-free intervals
Doubling it after one clean visit
Using the condition-3 column after every pass
explanation: A failure analysis decides whether the interval should be shortened. It does not automatically cut the interval every time a failure is reviewed. A risk-based change is also allowed. A longer interval can follow more than two intervals without problems, and that extension is written into the program. It is not the only way an interval may change. Manufacturer instructions still come first.

question: Device 27, in the ATS 7.9.1 list, is:
choices: Overvoltage
Undervoltage
Frequency
Directional power
explanation: 27 is undervoltage. 59 is overvoltage. 81 is frequency. 32 is directional power, which is not the thermal overload used on a motor. Learn the number before you read the one-line.

question: The motor thermal element in the ATS device list is 49. Device 32 is:
choices: The same thermal element
Directional power
A recloser count
A surge counter
explanation: 49 is thermal. 51 is time overcurrent. 32 looks at power direction and is the element you meet on a generator or a network, not the ordinary motor overload. ATS 7.15 points the motor starter at section 7.16, not at a 32 test.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1 (device 32, directional power; devices 49T and 49R, thermal)

question: An electromechanical overcurrent relay set on tap 3 picks up at 3.8 A. ATS 7.9.1 says you:
choices: Pass it, because it is the same tap number
Determine minimum pickup and hold it to the manufacturer’s tolerance
Always move the tap to 4 and do not retest
Always loosen the spring, which ATS names as the only adjustment
explanation: 3.8 on a tap of 3 is far enough away that you do not call it good without the manufacturer’s tolerance. ATS tells you to determine pickup. It does not say the fix is always the spring or always the next tap. Those adjustments are in the relay manual.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1 item 15 (device 51: minimum pickup and two timing points)

question: A test set that applies an AC voltage and separates the loss current by phase angle is used for:
choices: Insulation power factor or dissipation factor
A fall-of-potential ground test
A DC hipot only
A clamp-on ground loop
explanation: Power-factor and tan-delta sets measure charging current and loss. A megohmmeter is DC resistance. ATS calls for the power-factor test on transformer windings, and on other apparatus, in accordance with the test-set instructions.

question: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.23 covers automation and communications equipment. Which of these belongs to that work?
choices: Only the 51-to-86-to-52 trip path, with communications left out of the standard
Communication links, digital points, alarms, and settings files
A megohmmeter guard connection used in place of the network
A dissolved-gas sample drawn from the controller
explanation: ATS-2025 7.23 covers automation and communications equipment, including the communication links, the digital points, the alarms, and the settings files. Protective-relay section 7.9.2 adds optional checks of SCADA metering and status. Neither section is a lesson in how to address a PLC. The trip path from a 51 through an 86 to the breaker is still scheme logic, and a guard lead or an oil sample is a different test.

question: In a 51-to-86-to-52 trip path, the device that operates first is:
choices: The breaker trip coil
The lockout coil
The 51 overcurrent element
The close coil
explanation: The 51 must pick up before it can energize the 86. The 86 then latches and closes a contact that energizes the 52 trip coil. Resetting the breaker does not reset the 86. An a contact is open when its device is dropped out; a b contact is closed when its device is dropped out.

question: An a contact on a protective-relay scheme is:
choices: Closed while its device is de-energized
Open while its device is de-energized, and closed when that device is picked up
A transfer contact with both states at once
The guard lead of a megohmmeter
explanation: An a contact is open when its device is dropped out and closed when the device is picked up. Catalogs also call that a Form A contact. A b contact, also called Form B, is the opposite: closed when dropped out, which is why it is used as a close permissive. Resetting a breaker does not by itself reset an 86 that latched ahead of it.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (a and b contacts); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1

question: In the relay-catalog convention, Form A, Form B, and Form C contacts are:
choices: Instantaneous overcurrent, time overcurrent, and differential
Normally open, normally closed, and transfer
The same devices as 50, 51, and 87
Oil dielectric, interfacial tension, and power factor
explanation: Catalogs call Form A a normally open contact, Form B a normally closed contact, and Form C a transfer contact. Those letter names are a catalog convention, and ATS-2025 does not print them. On a schematic, still read the contact by what it does: an a contact is open when the coil is dropped out, and a b contact is closed when the coil is dropped out.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (relay catalog contact forms); not printed in ANSI/NETA ATS-2025

question: A close circuit supervised by two 86 b contacts will allow a close only when:
choices: Either lockout is still tripped
Both lockouts are reset, so both b contacts are closed
The 51 is picked up
One lockout is reset and the breaker is already closed
explanation: A b contact is closed only while its device is dropped out. An 86 that is still latched has opened its b contact and blocks the close. Resetting only one of two lockouts leaves the other contact open. The 51 operates first in a trip path; it is not the close permissive.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (b-contact close permissive); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1

question: NFPA 70B-2026 intervals for relays, conditions 1, 2, and 3, are:
choices: Electromechanical 36, 24, and 12 months; solid-state and microprocessor 60, 36, and 12 months
The same 12, 12, and 6 months for both
Electromechanical before each use
Microprocessor relays are exempt
explanation: Electromechanical relays are on the shorter row. Solid-state and microprocessor relays use 60, 36, and 12 months. The electrical table calls for pickup, three-point timing, and restraint or directional checks, and it does not print a percent tolerance.

question: Which check does NFPA 70B-2026 Table 35.3.5 aim at a microprocessor relay rather than at an electromechanical relay?
choices: Status and arc-reduction checks, with arc reduction per the manufacturer
Branch-to-frame insulation resistance and a zero check
A dissolved-gas sample of the relay case
Specific gravity
explanation: Electromechanical relays get the branch-to-frame insulation test and the zero check. Microprocessor relays get status and arc-reduction checks, and the arc-reduction test follows the manufacturer. Pickup and timing are on the table for the relays that have those elements. No timing tolerance is printed.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 35.3.5, on protective-relay tests, tells you to:
choices: Perform the tests the table lists, and follow the manufacturer's instructions for the relay
Apply a timing-tolerance percent printed in that table
Replace the timing points with a restraint check
Skip pickup and use only the zero check
explanation: The table names the tests. It does not print a manufacturer tolerance band and it does not give a percent of your own. Where the work depends on the relay, follow the manufacturer's instructions. Pickup, timing points, restraint or directional checks, and the inputs and outputs are tests on that list, not a substitute for those instructions.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 relay inspection includes settings checked against:
choices: The coordination study
The cable very-low-frequency menu
A battery specific-gravity sample
Table 15.3.5 trip time, which 70B does not print
explanation: Cases, displays, wiring, and settings are compared with the coordination study. Electromechanical relays also get a clearance check. Microprocessor events are documented. The electrical tests are pickup, three-point timing, and restraint or directional checks, still without a percent band.

question: On a one-line diagram, device number 52 is:
choices: An ac circuit breaker
A dc circuit breaker
A line switch
A lockout relay
explanation: 52 is an ac breaker, which closes and interrupts an ac power circuit in normal service and interrupts it under fault. A dc breaker is 72, a line switch is 89, and a lockout relay is 86. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.52.

question: On a relay schematic, device 86 is a device that:
choices: Trips and holds the equipment out of service until an operator resets it, locally or remotely
Resets itself as soon as the fault clears
Measures differential current
Recloses the breaker after a time delay
explanation: The lockout relay's job is to keep the equipment off until a person resets it. A self-resetting trip relay is device 94, and reclosing is device 79. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.86.

question: On a one-line diagram, device 89 is:
choices: A line switch, such as a disconnect, load-interrupter, or isolating switch, usually numbered only when it is motor operated or has electrical accessories
A frequency relay
A ground detector
A dc circuit breaker
explanation: 89 covers disconnecting, load-interrupter, circuit-switcher, and isolating switches. The guide notes the number normally is not needed unless the switch is electrically operated or has items like auxiliary switches or magnetic locks.

question: On a breaker trip schematic, what separates device 94 from device 86?
choices: 94 is a self-resetting tripping or trip-free relay. 86 holds the equipment locked out until an operator resets it
94 is hand-reset, and 86 is self-resetting
They are the same function with different numbers
94 is a dc breaker, and 86 is an ac breaker
explanation: 94 trips a breaker or contactor, lets other devices trip it immediately, or blocks immediate reclosing, and then resets on its own. 86 latches and requires a reset. Mixing them up changes how the scheme behaves after a trip. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.86 and 3.1.94.

question: Device 62 is a time-delay stopping or opening relay. On a relay drawing, 62BF is:
choices: A battery-float alarm
A bus-fault differential
A breaker-failure function with no current monitoring
A breaker-failure function that supervises with current detectors
explanation: The guide uses 62BF as breaker failure done purely on a timer, with no current check. Current-monitored breaker failure takes the suffix on device 50 instead, as 50BF. Device 2 is the matching time-delay starting or closing relay.

question: On a power circuit breaker schematic, a 52a auxiliary contact is:
choices: Open when the breaker is open (its reference position) and closed when the breaker is closed
Closed when the breaker is open
A contact on the switchgear housing that tracks rack position
A contact that opens only on a trip
explanation: An 'a' contact is open in the device's standard reference position and closes when the device changes state. A 'b' contact does the opposite. For a power circuit breaker, the reference position is main contacts open, so 52a follows the main contacts and 52b is the inverse. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 4.1 and Table 1.

question: On a drawout breaker schematic, the suffixes TOC and MOC mean:
choices: Truck-operated contact (on the housing, changes with rack position) and mechanism-operated contact (driven by the breaker mechanism)
Time overcurrent and maximum overcurrent
Trip output coil and motor operator coil
Top of cubicle and middle of cubicle
explanation: Both are auxiliary switches mounted on the stationary housing. TOC switches change with the breaker truck's position. MOC switches are moved by the breaker's operating mechanism. Neither is the breaker's own a/b auxiliary switch, which is a common troubleshooting mix-up. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.5.4 (TOC and MOC notes).

question: On a one-line drawing, the surge (lightning) arrester symbol belongs to the same family as:
choices: Fuse symbols
Current transformer symbols
Battery symbols
Gap symbols, such as horn gap, protective gap, sphere gap, and valve or film elements
explanation: IEEE 315 item 9.3 covers the arrester along with its gap and valve-element variants and their combinations. Fuses are 9.1 and breakers are 9.4. Knowing the arrester family helps you pick it out on a one-line drawing.

question: On a schematic battery symbol with no polarity marks, the positive terminal is:
choices: The short line
Whichever side is drawn on top
Not shown by the symbol
The long line
explanation: IEEE 315 says the long line of the battery or cell symbol is always positive. Polarity signs may be added, but they are not needed. This matters when you read dc control drawings before you check a trip circuit.

question: A schematic shows a chassis or frame connection symbol rather than the general ground symbol. That tells you:
choices: The conductor ties to a frame or chassis that may be at substantial potential relative to earth
The point is bonded directly to earth
The point is a protective earth for shock protection
The conductor is a neutral
explanation: IEEE 315 keeps three symbols apart: the general ground (a connection to earth, or to a structure acting as earth), the protective ground, and the chassis or frame connection. The chassis symbol does not promise earth potential, so do not treat it as a safety ground when you plan test connections.

question: During energization tests on a transformer differential, the magnetizing inrush current is best described as:
choices: A sine wave with no harmonics
Rich in harmonics, particularly the second, and not necessarily rich in every phase
Only a fifth-harmonic overexcitation problem
A differential current that restraint cannot see
explanation: Inrush violates the idea that current in equals current out, and it is full of harmonics, especially the second. Those harmonics are not always large in every phase. ATS 7.9.1 tells you to determine harmonic restraint on an 87. This clause is why that restraint exists. A scheme that only blocks during the instant of energizing is not enough, because inrush also follows faults and out-of-step closing.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1, device 87; ref. IEEE C37.91-2021, clause 6.5.3

question: A generator one-line shows a relay tagged 38 wired to RTDs on the shaft. That device is watching:
choices: Stator winding temperature
Bearing temperature or other bearing trouble
Field current
Phase sequence
explanation: Device 38 is the bearing protective device. It acts on high bearing temperature or other bearing problems such as wear. Winding temperature is device 49, field trouble is 40, and phase sequence is 47. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.38.

question: On a transformer control drawing, one thermal device is numbered 49 and another is numbered 26. What is the difference?
choices: 49 is for the load-carrying winding; 26 is for the apparatus or a liquid or other medium, such as top oil
49 is for the liquid; 26 is for the winding
They mean the same thing; the number depends on the manufacturer
49 is an alarm only and 26 always trips
explanation: 49 is the machine or transformer thermal relay, tied to the temperature of a load-carrying winding. 26 is the apparatus thermal device for the equipment itself or a liquid or other medium, which is why a top-oil gauge is a 26. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.26 and 3.1.49.

question: A substation panel has a horn-and-light relay numbered 74 and a window-type alarm panel numbered 30. Device 30 is:
choices: A self-resetting alarm relay
A bearing alarm
An annunciator: a manually reset device that gives separate visual indications when protective devices operate
A trip-circuit monitor
explanation: 30 is the annunciator relay. It is not reset automatically and shows separate indications for each protective device, and it can be set up to lock out. 74 is an alarm relay other than an annunciator. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.30 and 3.1.74.

question: A pump motor relay has an element numbered 37 enabled. It trips when:
choices: Current or power drops below its set value, for example a pump running dry
Current rises above its set value with no delay
Voltage drops below its set value
Frequency drops below its set value
explanation: 37 is undercurrent or underpower. It acts when current or power falls below a set value, which is how loss-of-load on a pump is caught. Undervoltage is 27, instantaneous overcurrent is 50, and underfrequency is 81. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.37.

question: The station battery feeds the dc panel through a breaker tagged 72 on the drawings. Device 72 is:
choices: An ac circuit breaker
A dc circuit breaker
A dc overcurrent relay
A load-resistor contactor
explanation: 72 is the dc circuit breaker, used to close and interrupt a dc power circuit and to clear dc faults. The ac breaker is 52, and a dc overcurrent relay is 76. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.72.

question: A local/remote selector switch on a breaker control panel, which changes which control circuit is in charge, would be numbered:
explanation: 43 is the manual transfer or selector device. It is operated by hand and moves control or potential circuits to change how the equipment is operated, such as local versus remote or auto versus manual. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.43.

question: A two-position switch on the panel allows closing the breaker in one position and blocks it in the other. Its device number is:
explanation: 69 is the permissive control device: one position allows the breaker or equipment to be closed or started, the other prevents it. 3 is a checking or interlocking relay, 25 is synchronism check, and 79 is reclosing. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.69.

question: A generator relay has a 78 element enabled. It is meant to act on:
choices: Loss of field
An unstable power swing (out of step), or a set phase-angle difference
Reverse power
Overfrequency
explanation: 78 is the phase-angle measuring relay. It trips for an unstable power swing or works at a set angle between two voltages, two currents, or a voltage and a current. Loss of field is 40, reverse power is 32, and frequency is 81. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.78.

question: A ground overcurrent relay is fed from a CT on the transformer neutral-to-ground connection. Another is fed from the residual of the three phase CTs. Which suffixes fit?
choices: Neutral CT: 51G. Residual: 51N
Neutral CT: 51N. Residual: 51G
Both are 51G
Both are 51N
explanation: The suffix G is preferred when the measured quantity is in the path to ground, like a CT on the neutral-to-ground lead. N is preferred when the element is in the residual of the phase CTs, across a broken delta, or derived inside the relay from the phase quantities. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.5, footnote to suffixes G and N.
reference: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.5 (suffixes G and N, footnote)

question: On a voltage regulator control drawing, the regulating device that holds voltage between close limits carries the number:
explanation: 90 is the regulating device. It holds a quantity such as voltage, current, power, speed, frequency, or temperature at a value or between close limits. 59 and 27 are over- and undervoltage, and 60 is voltage or current balance. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.90.

question: A feeder relay label reads 50/51. That means:
choices: One device doing two jobs: instantaneous and time overcurrent
The pickup is 50 A instantaneous and 51 A time delay
Relay 50 is backed up by relay 51 in a separate case
The 51 element is half the 50 setting
explanation: When one device does two important jobs, both numbers can be shown with a slash. 50/51 is a single device with an instantaneous element and an inverse-time element. The numbers are functions, not settings. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.7.

question: You are checking a schematic during a functional test. Unless a note says otherwise, the relay and switch contacts are drawn:
choices: In the state they take when the actuating device is de-energized or not operated
In their normal running state with the breaker closed
In whatever state the drafter chose
In the energized state
explanation: Standard practice draws each contact in the condition it has when its actuating device is de-energized or not operated. If a drawing shows contacts in the operated state, it is supposed to carry a clarifying note. Source: IEEE 315-1975 (R1993), 4.3.

question: Checking CT polarity on a drawing, you notice a tapped CT secondary. How many polarity marks should that secondary winding carry?
choices: One per tap
One for the whole winding, near one end
Two: one at each end
None, because taps make polarity meaningless
explanation: Polarity marks go near one end of each coil or winding, and only one mark per winding is allowed, even when it is tapped. Extra marks on taps are a drawing error. Source: IEEE 315-1975 (R1993), 1.6.3 note B.

question: On a fuse symbol where one end is drawn with a thicker line, the thick end shows:
choices: The load side
The supply side
A current-limiting fuse
A fuse with an alarm contact
explanation: The fuse symbol can mark the supply side with a thick line. A fuse with an alarm contact is a separate symbol. Source: IEEE 315-1975 (R1993), 9.1.1.1 and 9.1.2.

question: A meter circle on a generator synchronizing panel drawing is labeled SY. That instrument is a:
choices: Synchroscope
System voltmeter
Sync-check relay
Sequence-of-events recorder
explanation: Meter circles carry letters that name the instrument. SY is the synchroscope. A sync-check relay is device 25, which is a relay function, not a meter. Source: IEEE 315-1975 (R1993), 12.1, note A.

question: On a one-line diagram, a protective relay is drawn as a circle with a number inside, such as 87. The number is:
choices: The relay's catalog number
The device function number, which the symbol rules allow inside or next to the circle
The CT ratio
The setting in amps
explanation: Relay protective-function symbols can show the function with the device function number placed in the circle or next to it. That is why 50, 51, 87, and so on appear in circles on one-lines. Source: IEEE 315-1975 (R1993), 9.5.1.

question: In the symbol standard used for one-lines, the network protector:
choices: Has its own symbol, listed with the circuit breaker symbols
Uses the fuse symbol
Uses the disconnect switch symbol
Has no symbol and is shown as a box with text
explanation: The circuit breaker item group includes a separate network protector symbol, alongside the general breaker and the low-voltage air breaker symbols. Source: IEEE 315-1975 (R1993), 9.4.3.

question: During acceptance of a substation automation system with redundant communication paths, what does ATS require for the links?
choices: Only that the primary link is up
That links are operational and error free, and that failover to the redundant link is function tested, with failover time per the manufacturer
A hipot of the fiber
Only a visual check of the cabling
explanation: ATS has you verify every communication link is working and error free and function-test the failover of redundant links. Failover times are judged against the manufacturer's published data. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.23.B.4 and D.4.

question: How does ATS have you prove the digital outputs of an RTU or automation controller?
choices: By reading the output status bit on the HMI
By operating the controlled device with each output
By measuring output contact resistance
By checking the settings file
explanation: Seeing a status bit change is not enough. ATS has you verify each digital output by operating the device it controls, and outputs must work as designed. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.23.B.3 and D.3.

question: Two static (solid-state) overcurrent relays are coordinated in series without field calibration. Per IEEE 242-2001, what coordinating time interval range is reasonable, and why is it smaller than for electromechanical relays?
choices: 0.10 s to 0.15 s; breaker time is ignored
0.20 s to 0.30 s; there is no disk overtravel
0.35 s to 0.50 s; static relays are less accurate
1.0 s; static relays need extra margin
explanation: Table 15-1 builds the CTI from breaker opening time, relay overtravel, and tolerance: 0.35 s for electromechanical relays and 0.25 s for static relays, which have no overtravel. The guide says static relays allow 0.20 s to 0.30 s, and 0.30 s is a widely used average for field-tested electromechanical systems. Source: IEEE 242-2001, 15.5 and Table 15-1.

question: A 59 overvoltage element is set to pick up at 132 V. ATS 7.9.1 times it with a sudden application of 120% of pickup. The test voltage is:
explanation: 1.2 x 132 = 158.4 V. Applying the voltage suddenly at that level gives a repeatable operating time to compare with the setting. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1 (device 59).

question: Testing a reclosing relay (79) per ATS 7.9.1, which result shows the scheme works after the last unsuccessful shot?
choices: The relay goes to lockout and stops reclosing
The relay keeps reclosing until the fault clears
The relay resets to the first shot right away
The relay trips the upstream breaker
explanation: ATS has you check each reclose interval, the reset time, the close pulse, instantaneous-overcurrent lockout, and lockout after unsuccessful reclosing. Endless reclosing into a fault is exactly what lockout prevents. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1 (device 79).

question: Beyond pickup and slope, which characteristic is on the ATS 7.9.1 test list for a transformer differential (87) element?
choices: Maximum torque angle
Reclose interval
Harmonic restraint
Volts-per-hertz pickup
explanation: The 87 list covers operating pickup, restraint units, slope, and harmonic restraint. Maximum torque angle belongs to directional elements such as the 32. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1 (device 87).

question: A generator anti-motoring element (32) is tested per ATS 7.9.1. Which test is specific to it and not part of a 51 test?
choices: Timing at several multiples of tap setting
Instantaneous pickup
Finding the maximum torque angle
Time-dial verification
explanation: Directional power elements are checked for their operating characteristic and maximum torque angle. Timing at multiples of tap and time dial belong to inverse-time overcurrent. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1 (device 32).

question: Which drawing shows the course of a power system with single lines and graphic symbols, usually ignoring physical layout?
choices: One-line (single-line) diagram
Schematic (elementary) diagram
Wiring (connection) diagram
Panel layout drawing
explanation: IEEE 315 defines the single-line diagram as one that shows, by single lines and symbols, the course of a circuit or system and its component devices. It's the drawing for switching, isolation points, and protection zones. Source: IEEE 315-1975 (R1993), A4.1.1; Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., Ch. 1 (types of diagrams).
reference: IEEE 315-1975 (R1993), A4.1.1; Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., Ch. 1 (types of diagrams)

question: You need to trace why a breaker won't close from its control switch. Which drawing is meant for following a circuit's function regardless of where devices physically sit?
choices: One-line diagram
Site plan
Conduit and raceway schedule
Schematic (elementary) diagram
explanation: A schematic shows the electrical connections and functions of a circuit without regard to the size, shape, or location of the parts. It's the drawing for troubleshooting control logic: coils, contacts, and interlocks in order. Source: IEEE 315-1975 (R1993), A4.1.2.

question: You need to find which terminal block point a CT lead lands on inside a relay panel. Which drawing is built for that?
choices: One-line diagram
Wiring (connection) diagram
Schematic (elementary) diagram
Block diagram
explanation: A wiring or connection diagram locates and identifies devices, terminals, and interconnecting wires in an assembly. The schematic shows what the circuit does; the wiring diagram shows where the wire physically goes. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., Ch. 1 (types of diagrams).
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., Ch. 1 (types of diagrams)

question: A drawing has a chart showing which contacts of a control switch are closed in TRIP, NORMAL, and CLOSE. That is a:
choices: One-line diagram
Control sequence (truth-table) diagram
Wiring diagram
Elevation drawing
explanation: A control sequence or truth-table diagram lists the contact positions or connections made for each position of a control device. IEEE C37.2 shows charts of this kind for switch contacts on elementary diagrams. Source: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., Ch. 1 (types of diagrams); IEEE C37.2-2022, 4.5.2.
reference: Gill, Electrical Power Equipment Maintenance and Testing, 2nd ed., Ch. 1 (types of diagrams); IEEE C37.2-2022, 4.5.2

question: Under ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, what has to happen with the drawing packages at the end of commissioning?
choices: The original design set is returned to the engineer
Only the one-line needs updating
Drawings are optional if test reports are complete
They must be as-built; a complete set stays on site and a duplicate goes to the owner/operator
explanation: ECS-2024's documentation list says all applicable drawing packages shall be as-built, with a complete set left on site and a duplicate submitted to the owner/operator. Drawings that don't match the field are a hazard the next time someone switches. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024, 5.4 (documentation, drawing packages).

question: On an elementary diagram, how does IEEE C37.2 recommend showing a contact on a device with no de-energized position, such as a manual-automatic switch or a breaker-housing TOC switch?
choices: Drawn normally open, with a mark saying in which position it closes
Drawn normally closed with no label
Left off the drawing
Drawn in whatever position it was in during commissioning
explanation: Devices without a standard reference position should preferably be drawn normally open, and each contact identified by when it closes (for example A for automatic, M for manual, or the breaker position for a TOC). Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 4.5.3.

question: Nearly every ATS inspection list opens with 'compare equipment nameplate data with drawings.' The main reason is:
choices: To record serial numbers for warranty
To check the drawing title block is signed
To catch equipment that doesn't match the design before its settings and tests are based on wrong data
Because nameplates fade over time
explanation: Settings, test values, and protective device sizes all come from the drawings and studies. A wrong rating or ratio found at the nameplate step saves everything that would follow from it. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.A.1, 7.10.1.A.1, 7.6.3.A.1.

question: On an elementary diagram drawn to IEEE C37.2, how are a and b contacts shown?
choices: a contacts closed and b contacts open
Both as they are at the moment of the drawing's revision
b contacts closed and a contacts open (device at rest)
Both open, with a note
explanation: C37.2 has diagrams show b contacts closed and a contacts open. Read the drawing as the device at rest, then work out what changes when it operates. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 4.5.1.

question: A breaker auxiliary contact marked aa is:
choices: A contact that is closed whenever control power is on
A late b contact that opens after the main contacts
An early a contact: open at rest, closing as the mechanism operates
A latch-check switch that confirms the mechanism is latched
explanation: C37.2 4.2.1 defines aa as open in the non-operated position and closing when the mechanism moves, sometimes called an early a. bb is the early b. LC is the latch-check switch. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 4.2.1.

question: OUT101 := NOT(RB01 OR SV02). With RB01 = 0 and SV02 = 0, OUT101 is:
choices: 1 (asserted)
0 (deasserted)
It toggles each processing interval
Undefined until RB01 changes
explanation: The OR inside the parentheses is 0, and NOT 0 is 1. The output asserts only when neither input is asserted, which makes this a NOR gate. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.195 (Boolean NOT operator).
reference: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.195 (Boolean NOT operator)

question: In SELOGIC, which operator has the lowest precedence, so it is evaluated last unless parentheses say otherwise?
choices: AND
NOT
R_TRIG
OR
explanation: The precedence list runs from parentheses down through NOT, the edge triggers, math, comparisons, AND, and finally OR. So A OR B AND C means A OR (B AND C). Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Table 4.72.

question: SV05 := (SV05 OR IN101) AND (IN103 OR RB02). Once IN101 pulses on while the second group is true, what keeps SV05 asserted after IN101 drops?
choices: IN101 latching internally
SV05 feeding back into its own OR term (a seal-in)
A timer pickup delay that holds the output after the input drops
Nothing; SV05 drops when IN101 drops
explanation: This is a seal-in: the output feeds its own OR term, like a relay contact in parallel with the start button. It stays in until the AND term goes false. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.194 (parentheses operator example).
reference: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.194 (parentheses operator example)

question: How long is the output of R_TRIG IN101 asserted when IN101 goes from 0 to 1?
choices: As long as IN101 stays at 1
One processing interval
Until it is reset by a latch
One second
explanation: R_TRIG produces a one-interval pulse on a rising edge, which is why it's used to start event reports and counters without retriggering while the input stays on. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.195 (rising-edge operator).

question: A latch bit has SET and RST both asserted in the same processing interval. What state is the latch bit in?
choices: Asserted (1): set has priority
It toggles each interval
It holds whatever state it had before
Deasserted (0): reset has priority
explanation: For the SEL-751 latch switch, RST wins when both are true. Check this when a latch you expect to hold is being cleared by a reset term that stays on. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.191 (latch bits).

question: A latch bit drives an output contact, and the relay loses control power. What happens to the latch and to the contact?
choices: The latch is kept, but the contact drops until the relay restarts
Both the latch state and the output contact state are lost
The contact stays held closed through the outage
The latch resets to 0 every time power is lost
explanation: Unlike a mechanical latching relay, the output contact drops with control power. After initialization it returns to the latch state. The manual also warns that frequent latch writes wear the nonvolatile memory. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.190 to 4.192 (latch bits, nonvolatile state).
reference: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.190 to 4.192 (latch bits, nonvolatile state)

question: The math expression MV01 := 12 * IN101 + (MV01 + 1) * NOT IN101 runs each processing interval. With IN101 deasserted, MV01:
choices: Is held at 12 until reset
Resets to 0
Increases by 1 each execution
Doubles each interval
explanation: With IN101 = 0, the first term is 0 and NOT IN101 = 1, so MV01 becomes MV01 + 1. When IN101 asserts, MV01 is set to 12. This is an if/else built from NOT. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.195 (NOT in math equations).
reference: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), 4.195 (NOT in math equations)

question: Two relays need a contact that closes only when both a 27 undervoltage and a 62 timer have operated. In logic terms, the contacts are wired:
choices: In parallel, which is an OR
In series, which is an OR
In series, which is an AND
In parallel, which is a NOT
explanation: Series contacts pass current only when every contact is closed, which is AND. Parallel contacts pass current if any one closes, which is OR. The SELOGIC seal-in example shows the same OR/AND pattern. Source: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Table 4.72 and 4.194; IEEE C37.2-2022, 4.5.1.
reference: SEL-751 Instruction Manual (date code 20240329), Table 4.72 and 4.194; IEEE C37.2-2022, 4.5.1

question: Element pickup and timing on a new microprocessor relay all match the setting file, but no one has walked the internal logic against the owner's logic diagram. The technician wants to accept the relay. What should you do?
choices: Walk the internal scheme logic against the owner's narrative or logic diagram, and confirm that the settings and the logic still match the latest engineered files, before you accept the relay
Element tests are enough; internal logic is proven automatically when pickup is correct
Logic checks are only required on electromechanical relays
Accept the relay now and compare logic to the drawings after energization
explanation: ATS requires a check of the internal scheme logic against the owner's narrative or logic diagram, and it requires the settings and the logic to match the latest engineered files. Proving an element in isolation is not the same as proving the scheme. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.9.2.B.3 and 7.9.2.C.3.

question: A generator protective scheme must trip if the machine motors on a loss of its prime mover and power flows into the machine. Which IEEE C37.2 device is provided for that condition?
choices: Device 40, which is reserved for reverse-power conditions only
Device 87, which operates only on reverse power and never on differential current
Device 32, the directional power relay. IEEE C37.2 uses the example of reverse power when a generator motors after it loses its prime mover
Device 27, which is the standard reverse-power function
explanation: IEEE C37.2 lists device 32 as the directional power relay and gives the example of reverse power when a generator motors after it loses its prime mover. Device 40 is the field over/under-excitation relay, not the reverse-power function. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.32.

question: A synchronous generator needs a relay that will operate for abnormally high or low field current, or for an excessive reactive component of armature current that indicates abnormal field excitation. Which IEEE C37.2 device is that?
choices: Device 32, which is only a directional power relay
Device 24, which IEEE C37.2 assigns to field excitation only
Device 40, which IEEE C37.2 names the field over/under-excitation relay
Device 64, which is the standard loss-of-field function
explanation: IEEE C37.2 lists device 40 as the field over/under-excitation relay. It operates for unusual or failed field current, or for reactive armature current that points to a field-excitation problem. That is the identify-level function used for loss-of-field and overexcitation field problems. Deeper setting practice is left to a later generator-protection source. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, 3.1.40.

question: A trip output is programmed as 50 AND 67, with an 86 contact in series so that once the lockout is up the trip stays up. During a test the 50 and 67 elements both assert, but the breaker does not trip because the 86 was still reset and a wiring error held its series contact open. What should you conclude?
choices: The relay has failed because any asserted 50 should trip the breaker by itself
The internal elements asserted, but the scheme logic and trip path still have to be proved end-to-end, including the 86 series contact
Once 50 and 67 are picked up, the 86 contact can be ignored
Boolean AND is only used in SCADA, not in trip circuits
explanation: Level IV theory includes Boolean logic in protection and control. An AND condition requires every input to be true. A series 86 contact is another required true condition in the trip path. Proving the elements in isolation is not the same as proving the scheme. Verify internal logic and the trip path together before you accept the installation. Source: IEEE C37.2-2022, Clause 3 and device 86; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.9.2; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.B.2.
reference: IEEE C37.2-2022, Clause 3 and device 86; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.9.2; ANSI/NETA ETT-2026, 8.4.2.B.2

question: A synchronous generator's field breaker opens while the unit is still tied to the system. On the generator P-Q diagram, where does operation move, and what may the machine do if the system can still supply enough vars?
choices: Operation moves into the first quadrant, which is the overexcited motoring region, and the unit always stays in synchronism
Loss of field drives the unit into the second quadrant as a synchronous condenser, which is a stable, intended operating mode
The change is instantaneous and always trips the unit on overcurrent before any reactive interchange can develop

Operation moves into the fourth quadrant, with the system supplying the missing reactive power. If the system can feed those vars without a steep voltage decline, the unit may keep running as an induction generator; otherwise it can fall out of step
explanation: Normal generation is slightly lagging power in the first quadrant. When excitation is reduced or lost, current moves into the fourth quadrant and the system has to supply the missing reactive power. Synchronous machines have reduced stability there. If the system can feed enough inductive vars without a steep voltage decline, the unit may keep running as an induction generator; otherwise it can fall out of step. The change is not instantaneous. An early alarm may let the operator restore the field before a shutdown is required. Source: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.11.1.
reference: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.11.1

question: You are reviewing a single-zone loss-of-field (40) distance setting intended only to detect complete loss of excitation. Which characteristic does Blackburn describe for that complete-loss setting?
choices: A first-quadrant mho set to 120% of the machine capability curve, with no intentional time delay
A circle in the fourth quadrant with a diameter on the order of Xd, and with the top of the circle 50% to 75% of Xd' below the origin, typically tripping in about 0.2 to 0.3 s to shut the unit down
A circle centered at the origin with radius Xs, used only to alarm, never to trip
A var-type relay set at 45 degrees into the overexcited region, tripping in 10 s to 1 min
explanation: For a total field collapse, the distance element is a smaller fourth-quadrant circle. Its diameter is on the order of the synchronous reactance Xd, and the top of that circle sits 50% to 75% of the transient reactance Xd' below the origin. A trip in about 0.2 to 0.3 s is used when the unit is to be shut down completely. A larger circle, with a directional unit and often undervoltage supervision, is the setting used when partial as well as complete loss must be detected. Source: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.11.1, setting mode 1.
reference: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.11.1, setting mode 1

question: A two-zone loss-of-field scheme uses a wide 40 characteristic, a directional element, and an undervoltage element that drops out in the 87% to 80% band of rated voltage. The impedance is inside the circle, but terminal voltage is still healthy. What trip logic does Blackburn describe?
choices: Trip instantaneously whenever the impedance is inside the large circle, regardless of voltage

If the system can supply vars without a significant voltage drop, start an alarm and a delayed trip, typically 10 s to 1 min. If voltage falls below the undervoltage setting, trip in about 0.2 to 0.3 s
Block the 40 function entirely while voltage remains above 80%, and rely only on the small complete-loss circle
The undervoltage unit is used only to supervise motoring (32), not loss of field
explanation: The wider 40 characteristic is intended to see low, partial, or complete field loss, and a directional element keeps nearby faults and stable swings from operating it. Where used, an undervoltage element drops out in the 87% to 80% band and supervises the scheme. If the system can still feed vars without a large voltage decline, the scheme alarms so the operator can try to restore field; typical delays are 10 s to 1 min. If voltage falls below the undervoltage dropout, a trip is started in about 0.2 to 0.3 s. Large, important units often run both the small and the wide 40 settings. Source: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.11.1, setting mode 2.
reference: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.11.1, setting mode 2

question: A steam-turbine generator (condensing type) is still closed onto the system after its stop valves have shut. What motoring power, as a percent of nameplate kW, does Blackburn quote as typical to keep that machine spinning at synchronous speed with no prime-mover input, and what relay is recommended as a supplement to the machine's own detection?
choices: About 50% or more of nameplate kW, the same figure quoted for a gas turbine, so a coarse 32 pickup is adequate
About 25% of nameplate kW, the diesel-engine figure, with no need for a supplementary 32
Steam units do not motor; only hydro units need reverse-power protection because of cavitation
About 1% to 3% of nameplate kW into the machine. Add a backup 32 reverse-power element; typical microprocessor sensitivities can be as low as 1 mA, with an operating time of about 2 s
explanation: If the prime mover is removed while the generator stays online with the field excited, the system will motor the unit at synchronous speed. That overheats steam turbines and can cavitate hydro runners. Blackburn lists typical reverse-power values to spin the machine at synchronous speed with no input: condensing steam 1% to 3%, noncondensing steam 3% or more, hydro 0.2% to 2% or more, diesel about 25%, and gas turbine 50% or more. A supplementary 32 is recommended even though the machine control has its own detection. Microprocessor relays can be as sensitive as 1 mA, and the operating time can be about 2 s. Source: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.12.1.
reference: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.12.1

question: A generator is off the system and its speed is being changed during a start or shutdown. Voltage is still near rated. Why is a volts-per-hertz (24) function, rather than a plain overvoltage element, the right overexcitation protection, and what two-level settings does Blackburn suggest as a supplement to the machine controls?
choices: Generator voltage is proportional to frequency and flux, so pickup should stay constant on a V/Hz basis. A typical supplement is about 110% of rated to alarm and then trip in about 1 min, and about 120% of rated to trip in about 6 s, preferably from a separate VT
A plain 59 overvoltage element is preferred because flux is independent of frequency during start-up
A single 24 set at 150% of rated voltage with no time delay is the suggested supplement
Volts-per-hertz protection is only required after the unit is synchronized, so it should be blocked until the breaker is closed
explanation: Machines and transformers already run near the knee of the saturation curve, so a modest overvoltage produces large exciting current and damaging flux. A particularly dangerous window is while the unit is off the system and speed is changing. Voltage tracks frequency and flux, so overvoltage protection should hold a constant pickup versus V/Hz. Blackburn suggests two-level 24 units as a supplement to the generator controls: about 110% of rated voltage to alarm, then trip after about 1 min, and about 120% of rated to trip after about 6 s. A dedicated VT supply is preferable so a blown metering-VT fuse cannot operate the 24. Source: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.12.2.
reference: Blackburn and Domin, Protective Relaying, 4th ed., 8.12.2

question: A unit is on turning gear when its generator breaker is closed into an energized bus. Why may the usual stator protection not be enough, and what additional scheme does Blackburn describe?
choices: The generator differential (87) always covers inadvertent energization, so no added function is required
A 32 motoring element set at 50% of nameplate is the preferred replacement for any directional overcurrent in this case

Some protection is impaired or unavailable at low frequency. Additional protection is a 67 directional inverse-time overcurrent element in each phase, looking into the generator, typically picked up at about 0.5 pu current and operating in about 0.25 s at 2.0 pu, with prompt opening of adjacent breakers by breaker-failure or remote trip
The correct response is to rely only on the 25 sync-check and leave adjacent breakers closed
explanation: Accidentally energizing a generator can happen on turning gear, while coasting, at standstill, or after a bad synchronize. Ordinary machine protection will catch some of these events, but not every case, especially when performance falls off at low frequency.
